utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may address the Court. I would like to clarify the confusion that happened yesterday maybe with the dates and what happened with the transcript. There was a mistake in the transcript when I addressed to the Court and I mentioned the date as being April 2000 for the events that happened in the firing range. Your Honours, what happened is, with the firing range, the exact dates are on the -- the events happened in April 1999. On 24 May 2000, the witness went to the site and visited with members -- with representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor; and on the 12th of June, he provided a statement about the facts. And the point is I think the confusion and also created by the accused with several questions caused the mistake with the dates. But the right event -- and that is absolutely clear in both statements, the dates and the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It was the summary, I'm afraid, Ms. Romano, which was confusing.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It had the wrong date in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: That was a typo on the summary provided to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, could you be careful, in future, to see it doesn't --

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we must allow time for the accused to have further cross-examination to clarify the point. The cross-examination will be limited to questions about the exhumation at the firing range and the statement which was made about it, since there was confusion yesterday when he was asking questions about it. But first, Mr. Tapuskovic, is there anything else you want to ask of this witness, since you were stopped?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll assess that after the cross-examination by Mr. Slobodan Milosevic, by your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, if you want to ask any more questions about the statement and the firing range, now that the date has been clarified, you can do so. The issue which you were raising appears to be this: Why was it that in the first statement that was made to the Prosecutors there was no mention of the firing range?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, first of all, I would like to say something about what we just heard from this other side. Even if it were written in the statement that way, I wonder what the purpose of cross-examination is if not, inter alia, of course, to work in the interest of finding out the truth, inter alia challenging what the statement says. However, I wish to draw your attention to the following: An addendum was provided yesterday to Ali Gjogaj's statement, and it says: "I, Ali Gjogaj, would like to add the following to the statement that I gave: Number 1, the statement dated the 27th of February 2000 and the 1st of March, 2000 inserted after the first paragraph on page 1," then colon. It says: "This statement refers to events in April and May 1999 when the police sent me to assist the exhumation of bodies in the village of Orahovac, and Zrze, Dushanova, Prizren, et cetera other locations where these bodies were to be buried." So this addendum, this correction has to do with those things that we established yesterday, that we established had happened. The police were taking them to the hospital for examination, then afterwards buried them. Although when you insisted that these were mass graves, the witness answered that everybody was buried in an individual grave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I did not insist. I suggested, no more than that. It wasn't clear. The witness clarified it. But go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I asked how come 13 graves for 60 bodies, and then you said it was mass graves. So we clarified that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, look, we are here with the witness. The witness is here to finish his examination. Do you have any more questions for him or not? If not, I will ask him a question and then we'll let him go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Further cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gjogaj, please, yesterday you stated here under oath - we heard it in the microphone - did we state yesterday that the exhumations at the firing range that you refer to when you mentioned refrigerator truck, et cetera, did all this happen in the spring of 2000? Is that so or is that not so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If he did, it was due to confusion. It's my recollection that he didn't and it was counsel who suggested that to him. Now, look, Mr. Gjogaj, there's one point here. The point -- I'm going to put it because otherwise we're just going to waste further time. There's one point. You made a statement, you will remember, in March -- May -- just a moment, just a moment. I am asking the witness a question. Don't interrupt. You made a statement in May -- March, rather, 2000. You did not mention the firing range. Do you follow the point? Do you follow the point? You didn't mention that to a later statement. Can you help us how that came about? There may be an explanation, but can you explain?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I continue with my questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I want to hear an answer from the witness. Mr. Gjogaj, do you understand the point? You made two statements. Do you remember making statements to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. In the first one, you only dealt with Pusto Selo, taking the bodies from Pusto Selo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It wasn't until a second statement, made a few months later, that you dealt with the firing range.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, the question is: Why in the first statement did you not cover the firing range too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because when we gave the first statement, they first of all came and asked about Pastaselle and then later they asked about the firing range.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to object, Mr. May. Precisely the fact that this was not mentioned in the first statement and that the Prosecution insisted subsequently that this other thing happened at the same time when the first thing happened, which is highly unlikely, that is why I suspected that we were not referring to the same time, and that's why I asked Mr. Gjogaj to confirm when the firing range was topical, and that was the spring of 2000. And all of us in this courtroom heard this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So please, Mr. Gjogaj, did you confirm yesterday that these events occurred in the spring of 2000? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The event happened in the spring of 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember that yesterday you said it happened in the spring of 2000?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, there's no point arguing about what was said yesterday. It may well be -- we will have to look at the transcript. It may well be that he did, in which case we can draw a conclusion about it. But wait a minute. But it may be that he was confused by your questioning, which is quite possible. Now, we will have to come to a conclusion about it when we've read the transcript. I don't think there's much point going on arguing with the witness as to what he said. Now, is there anything more you want to ask him?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not think it is argument if I ask the witness whether he remembers that he said yesterday that the event occurred in the spring of 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there anything else you want to ask him?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, after the hearing was over, Mr. Gjogaj, who did you talk to out of all the people here? With how many people did you talk here?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where are you talking about? What people?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking since yesterday when we broke off, when the hearing was over yesterday, sometime around 2.00 in the afternoon, until this morning, who did you talk to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's much too general a question. Is the point this: Do you want to find out whether he talked to anyone from the Prosecution? Is that the point, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. Of course. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I'm just asking you who you talked to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is far too general a question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, it is not far too general, and I do not see why this is not a legitimate question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Because it's far too general. I've given you the answer. The question is this, Mr. Gjogaj: Did you talk to anybody from the Prosecution during the adjournment? That means overnight, since we were last in court together.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did you talk to any of the investigators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you talk to anyone, Mr. Gjogaj?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: About this case. The point is, did you talk to anybody about the case or about your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did not talk to anyone at all since yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. The only point is did he talk to anybody about the case, and the answer is no. Now, unless you've got some further questions, it's going to be brought to an end. Relevant questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gjogaj, I do have a question. What are the reasons for your change of statement since yesterday until today, overnight? What are the reasons for that? Why did you say yesterday the year 2000 and why do you say 1999 today? There is a difference. There is a one-year difference. So what are the reasons for the change?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're going back to the same point again which is arguing about what he said yesterday. Now, he's given his evidence. We have the transcript of it, we can all read it and draw such conclusions as are proper. Mr. Tapuskovic, have you got any questions you want to ask the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, I think that this should be clarified, an additional point. In both statements, it is stated that both these events were in the month of April 1999. That's what it says in his statements, both of them. Did both events that he spoke of today distinctly, did both occur in April?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think you'll find the first statement refers to April or May. First of all, it refers to spring.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The clarification is April or May. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. As for the second statement, he says unequivocally the month of April. This is what it says here, the month of April. He doesn't refer to May at all. That is paragraph number 4 in the second statement. Now, in addition to that, I'm interested in the following: He said that what he did in both cases, as he said, he worked with and he mentioned names, Buda, Shefki Salihu, Xhevdet Mazreku, Isuf Krasniqi, and also he said that the same was -- that these same people were engaged during this other event that took place. Can he say who he worked with the first time and who he worked with the second time? Further questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gjogaj, you said that both times the same people, absolutely the same people were together with you. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you sure that there were two events?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Any re-examination, Ms. Romano?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Gjogaj, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are three very short administrative matters in open session, one very short matter in private session, with your leave. The three matters in open session: First, K30 will now be giving evidence without protection. Second, the Chamber requested some details about disclosure of expert witnesses two days ago. That information is now in the form of a schedule similar to but more detailed than the general schedule you get and is now coming your way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: While you're dealing with expert reports, we've been looking at that, and it's not clear from the Rules, or indeed from our orders, as to whether they should be translated or not, and I think the view you've been taking is that they shouldn't be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In fact the view we've been taking is that by Rule they don't have to be but in all cases we're having them translated and the only problem is one of priority with CLSS for a document which isn't the subject of regulation, but we're getting them translated as soon as we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The issue, then, that we have to resolve is how much time has the accused got with them in his own language.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: They are disclosed in English to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And as soon as may be, given the pressures on CLSS in B/C/S, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may have an impact on the timing of witnesses, that's the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can understand. You will see that -- it may be that when the schedule comes your way, you will be particularly interested in what is said there about Philip Coo and the dating of the provision of B/C/S for him, which is obviously quite --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But he at least is a local witness, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exactly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If it was necessary for him to go back, could you fill the gap? I'm merely speculating.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll let you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that's the second point, and here comes the schedule. And I'll let you know, either personally or by someone else, where there will be any problem in filling the gap so far as Mr. Coo is concerned should the 16th of July be judged too early in relation to the provision of the B/C/S translation, but that's still two weeks away so there's a good long time. The third point: Mr. Hendrie. Mr. Hendrie is subject of arrangements to fly here tonight in order that he may be further cross-examined by the accused tomorrow. It's been quite inconvenient for Mr. Hendrie to obtain release from his employment to get here. My intention, in accordance with normal practice, would be not to ask him any particular questions myself about the topics upon which he should have been cross-examined but simply to tender him for further and appropriate cross-examination in light of the line that the accused has taken with later witnesses, and in particular with Ambassador Walker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a litigant in person. The usual Rules have got to be applied in a relevant way. A litigant in person may find it much more difficult to put the questions. It's more difficult for the Court if they're not put accurately, so it may be better if you put them and he can cross-examine on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well, then. That's very helpful. We've been obviously cautious about alerting him to the detail of what might be raised, and although he is aware, I think in general terms of the topic that will be covered, it had been my intention not to go through matters with him or, rather, to have Mr. Ryneveld go through matters with him in advance of his coming, but if the court's happy that we should do that, then he will be briefly prepared with his photographs and it will be up to the accused to deal with the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then can I -- the last matter, literally one minute in private session, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into private session

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat. Examined by Ms. Romano:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, can you state your full name for the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Halit Berisha, born on 5th of August, 1940, in Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's your profession, Mr. Berisha?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I'm a teacher of mathematics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, you provided the Office of the Prosecutor with a statement on 17 [sic] of August, 2001; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: On 17th of August, 2000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Are you sure?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can I have the witness shown the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness see the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: -- statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, can you please look at the date of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Excuse me. I have the Albanian version. I think I gave the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On 27th of August, 2001.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berisha. Mr. Berisha, on 13 March 2002, in Suva Reka, you remember attending a meeting with a presiding officer of the Registrar of this Tribunal, and at that opportunity you have -- you read your statement or you had the statement read to you, and you confirmed the contents of your statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After, Mr. Berisha, when you arrived here in The Hague, you also made a couple of corrections to your statement that I will go to in a minute. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The amendment is to page 4, paragraph 1, line 5 of the English version. The witness -- this is not included to the 92 bis procedure, was not included when the 92 bis procedure was done. And what the witness wants to correct, that part should read: "On that day, we left due to an offensive that occurred from Musutiste towards Buzhalle. My brother and family drove towards Albania via Prizren. The police stopped them and told them to go back to Savrove. Me and two of my sons hid in woods near Buzhalle. Two days later, we were reunited in Savrove where we remained for two days before returning to Suva Reka." And the statement continues: "I went to the woods with my two sons on 7 April 1999." Are these the corrections that you made when you arrived here?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. One I -- one correction I made was that it said that I met them after my return from Prizren. I didn't meet them in Prizren, but I met them in the village of Savrove after my return from Prizren.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berisha.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: At this point, the Prosecution wants to submit the statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 240 for the original version and 240A for the redacted version.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The witness is a Kosovar Albania. He was elected president of the municipality of Suva Reka on 24 May, 1989 and held that position until 5 April 1991 when he was forcefully removed from his office by members of the Serb Assembly of Suva Reka and the Serb secret police. On that occasion, the witness was shown a document from the Serb Assembly in Belgrade ordering him and other Albanians --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecutor please read slowly, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I apologise. I will read slow. The witness was unemployed from that date until 8 October, 1999 when he was reinstated into the municipality of Suva Reka as the vice-president. The witness describes the events from 24 March 1999 until 21st May 1999. He relates his knowledge of the massacre of the extended Berisha family on the 26th March 1999. He describes the increased movements of Serb forces in Suva Reka. He notes that the forces were wearing different colour uniforms and snipers were positioned in buildings around the town. The snipers would fire at Kosovar Albanian civilians, making movement very difficult. Around 6.30 on the 25th March, 1999, the witness spoke with family members for the Kuci and Ramadan Berisha families who were fleeing past his house. He was told that people near their home --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down a little.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Sorry. He was told that people near their homes had been killed and homes looted. On 26 March 1999, his brother Jashar left for work at about 12.20 p.m. He rang the witness's home, stating that people had been killed at the shopping centre. The witness gathered family members and fled. Later that day, he rang his brother at work and told him that the family Berisha members Sedat, Nexhat and Bujar had been killed by Serb police and that he had heard shooting, explosions, and screams from the shopping centre. On 28 March 1999, the witness heard an explosion and saw the minaret at the mosque destroyed. Later that evening, a Serb policeman neighbour came to his home and told him that he must go to Albania or paramilitaries would kill him. The witness and some family members headed for Prizren. They were stopped by Serb police who ordered them to go back. The witness and his two sons went into hiding in the woods for almost a month before joining his wife at the house of a family member. His wife told him that their home had been looted and vandalised. On 21st May 1999, police again came to his home and ordered him to leave for Albania, stating: "You have 15 minutes to leave for Albania or you will never see this land again." The witness left with family members in two vehicles and joined a convoy of approximately 5.000 people going towards Albania. The vehicles had been organised by the police in the centre of the town for those with no transport. At the border IDs, licenses and registration plates were removed by the police. On 23 June 1999, the witness returned to Kosovo. Annexed to the witness's statement are a number of documents found on his return, some downloaded from a floppy disk found in the premises of a local business and others located in the municipality building. That's all, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Turning to the documents, they appear, from the statement, to be documents related to the VJ in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If you'd like, I can ask the witness to give more details about the attachments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think we need more details. We can see them here. They are a series in relation to that particular topic, units of the VJ and the like. Yes. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just now received this pile of documents that are being introduced through this witness, and in this past minute I've looked through it and I fail to understand the purpose of this heap of paper, list of conscripts, list of motor vehicles, decisions of the Municipal Assembly about current everyday matters, lists of drivers and so on. Kindly explain to me the meaning of this and why am I receiving now this heap of paper which is now completely stripped of any value?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not for the Court to explain. It's a matter which the Prosecution should deal with. Ms. Romano, perhaps you could briefly, since the accused has raised it, assist us as to what you say the relevance of these documents about the VJ and Suva Reka are.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all I would like to clarify that that is not the first time the accused has received these documents. They have been disclosed before. All the documents that refer to this witness have been disclosed previously. These documents are documents - I can ask the witness also to clarify the Court - are the documents that when he returned to Kosovo, he found and they are relevant to the situation of the village at that time. They will be referred later on into -- when our military analyst will come and give the report what is the relevance and where the composition of the forces at the time. They also refer to decisions that he refer in his statement about what happened when he was dismissed, when he was -- just a second, Your Honour. That -- when he held the position, he was the president of the municipality of Suva Reka, and he was -- he was removed from his position. So some of the documents also that he annexed are referring to this fact that he mentioned in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So the relevance can be summarised as referring to the various units which were in Suva Reka which is said to have been the scene at least of one massacre, as said, and therefore is relevant as to what units were present in the town. And the other matter, if I may say of less relevance, with due respect to the witness, are matters concerning disputes which were occurring when he was in the municipality and his dismissal. No doubt you would say relevant as to the prejudice which existed and discrimination which existed against the Kosovo Albanians at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Exact. One more point, Your Honour, is that he provide also a list of members of the civil -- the local Civil Defence. That will also be subject of analysis of -- in the military report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Now, Mr. Milosevic, have you any questions of the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I most certainly do. I'm just trying to find some of these documents that would help me and perhaps could be clarified by the witness. All right. Let's not waste time. In view of the multitude of paper I've been served with, I don't know whether it's logical to have 92 bis apply to this witness and the limitation of my time. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Berisha, are you a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I'm not a member of any political party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in what political parties are the members of your family involved?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: No member of my family is a member of any political party. I have six sons, grown up, married; I have daughters-in-law, but not one of them is involved in a political party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You say that you were president of the municipal Assembly of Suva Reka from the 24th of May 1989 to the 5th of April, 1991. Who elected you from April, 1989?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: On 24th of May, 1989, I was elected by the Assembly of the municipality of Suva Reka, the delegates of the Assembly. And also in the October 1999 elections, I was again elected by members of the Assembly. Until 5th of April when, under a decision by the Serbian Assembly and on the proposal of the council of the Socialist Party of Suhareke, I was dismissed by force. And on the 5th of May, I was thrown out of my office. This was in 1991. There were five people who came from Belgrade and three local people who took over these positions. Among them there was Bobek Vuksanovic, Tomislav Borisavljevic, a local man, and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please don't give me such long answers. From the explanation you are giving, somebody could come to the conclusion that violence was used against you. Was that the case?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: There was no physical violence but I was told that I should get out of my office because I was no longer chairman of the municipality. It was psychological violence because the Serbian Assembly was not legitimate and didn't have any authority to dismiss me as chairman of the municipality. Only the Assembly that elects you can dismiss you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: The Assembly of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are talking about being replaced, and you don't mention the reasons. By sheer chance, I found in this heap of paper a draft proposal where they say they are addressing the government of the Republic of Serbia. They are writing to the government. And they said they had considered the situation in this municipality and came to the conclusion, due to the well-known events, support for the Kacanik constitution, and failure to abide by the decisions of the Assembly of Serbia, they are proposing that the president of the Assembly of Suva Reka be replaced. And this decision was indeed made, I suppose. If this draft proposal was really sent to the government, then forwarded to the Assembly, and you were replaced in due course. What is illegal about that?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: It was illegal because only the Assembly that elects you can dismiss you, and I was elected by the Assembly of Suhareke and not the Assembly of Serbia. This is why it's illegal. And there was no grounds for this step. But the main reason was to eliminate all Albanians from positions in the municipality, even though the proportion of the population in the municipality was 95 per cent Albanian, only 5 per cent Serbs, and a few Romanies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha --

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... was to take over power.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have just said that the purpose was to eliminate all Albanians from leading positions. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: [No translation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Berisha, that, for instance, the day before yesterday we read here from a book not by our witness but by the other side's witness, Wolfgang Petritsch, about officials of the Socialist Party of Serbia who were killed in 1998, who were Albanians, including presidents of municipal boards - that is, people who were at the same level as you were, ethnic Albanians - so could anyone possibly draw the conclusion that there was an intention to eliminate Albanians whereas in 1998 and 1999 there were Albanians in leading positions? Do you know that? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just one moment, Mr. Berisha. First of all, the witness cannot comment on what Mr. Petritsch said in evidence two days ago. He wasn't here and he can't comment on it. What you can put to him is that there was no discrimination at the time and Albanians were in leading positions. Now, Mr. Berisha, that is the suggestion made to you. It's for you to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From -- from the time when I was dismissed as municipal chairman down to 1998, no people were killed who were a part of the Serbian power structure. There was no murder at all. Down to the beginning of the war in 1998. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is my time limited to 45 minutes, Mr. May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider that, but start out on that basis. If you need more time, we'll look at the clock.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Then I have to hurry up. I'll skip some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you were allegedly replaced. You also mentioned Vuksanovic, a doctor, and Tomislav Borisavljevic, a secretary, and three members of the secret service. So who was it who replaced you? Was it the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia that you mentioned or were they members of the secret service? What's all the mystery about?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: They were brought by the decision of the Serbian Assembly, and three of them were members of the Serbian police secret service, and two of them belonged to the Serbian Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So two of them were deputies, right?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I didn't know them. I don't know their names. I don't know their names at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how do you know that those other people were members of the secret service?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Some members of the Municipal Assembly knew them, the three. I didn't know them, but these workers who worked in the Assembly, they -- they identified them as members of the Serbian secret service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, you mean those were some local policemen in your area. All right. Well, you say your people who worked in the Assembly knew them. Let's not waste any more time on this. You say Bobek Vuksanovic, who was president of the Suva Reka Assembly after you, was killed on the 14th of April, 1999. Do you know who killed him?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: His real name is Bobek Vuksanovic, and he's the son of Ymer Shetra, and his mother was a Vuksanovic. He was an illegitimate child and went to school and grew up in Suhareke, but I don't know who killed him on 14 April, 1999. But I do know that he was the commander of the Crisis Staff in Suhareke, and I know, as I have been told, that he was wearing a camouflage military uniform when he was killed and he was not killed as a doctor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I asked -- since you remembered the date when he was killed, I thought you knew who killed him, but you don't know, do you?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: You mentioned the date, and I don't know who killed him because I wasn't in Suhareke at the time because I was in the village of Savrove at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understood that this date is indicated in your statement, but let's not dwell on this. Do you know under what circumstances he was killed or where?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I only heard that he was killed. I don't know the circumstances. But I can repeat again that he was the commander of the Crisis Staff in Suhareke municipality from 1998 onwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while you were president of the Municipal Assembly from 1989 to 1991 in a variety of situations when you had your rules of procedure governing floods, crisis, traffic regulations, et cetera, were you the commander of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: According to the Statutes of the municipality, yes. But in 1998, it wasn't mayor of the municipality. It was a person called Radic. He wasn't mayor of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You claim that when you were being replaced, your pistol was taken away from you, the pistol that you had received as president of the Assembly for your personal protection. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: No. My pistol was taken on the 5th of August, 1990 when I was mayor of the municipality. It was taken away by -- under the order of someone from Belgrade. I don't know his name. There was something about recruiting young people. And in front of the defence, public defence building, which is across from the city hall, there were three policemen in armed vests, and they brought an invitation or an order telling me officially to -- relieving me of my duties as -- that was on the 5th of August, 1990. I was, at that time, mayor of the municipality. The position of a mayor at that time --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't understand a word you're saying, Mr. Berisha. You say that on the 5th of April, 1991, you were replaced. Now you say that it was the 5th of August.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: On the 5th of August, they took away my pistol. 1990. 5th of August, 1990. 1990, the 5th of August, that was when they took away my pistol. Whereas on the 5th of April, 1991, I was thrown out of office, of my office. They are two different dates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So at the time when your pistol was taken away from you, you were president of the Assembly, right?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the police thought you shouldn't have a gun?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Well, the police commander was the person who had decided -- who decided everything. The role of the mayor was so small in comparison that it was actually -- he decided everything. He had -- the police had all power in town. It was a totalitarian state, a totalitarian police state at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Using this example, you will have difficulty explaining this. Do you know a single country where the police does not issue licenses for weapons? Is there any country where a licence is not required?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's an irrelevant comment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where I come from in Yugoslavia, the police issues, indeed, licenses for firearms. They did so in the past and they do so nowadays. That's nothing new.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In addition to that pistol, did you have any other weapons?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I didn't need any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you on the 24th of March, 1989?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: In my own home in Suhareke. My house is behind the Assembly building, the post office, and the court office. There are three buildings next to each other and my house is behind these three buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So on the 24th of March, when the NATO aggression started, you were in Suva Reka in your own home; right?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that on that day you saw Serb soldiers in the church bell of the -- of the area and on the terrace of the post office building. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Police? Not 24th of March. In the police station, one, there was always a mortar, a large-calibre mortar in front of the police station, positioned there. The second was in the belfry of the church, and the Serbs had built a platform out of planks where the bell is, and there were four snipers there in commanding positions. And then below, the post office has a balcony, and they were on the post office balcony. And down below, further down, there is the department store, and the police were stationed above the department store, with a view of a large portion of the city centre. And they were stationed in the wine cellar. And from the villages of Sllapuzhan, Rreshtan, and they were stationed at the old post office in Suhareke, and above the post office, they were positioned in an apartment building known as Kula, beyond the health centre. And they were also stationed above the Balkan Hotel. Not the factory but the hotel. That is where police forces were stationed in the town of Suhareke. From about the end of May, of April 1998. And the largest reinforcements came in March 1999. And then it was impossible to pass --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, if you would just deal with the questions, please, and if there are more questions about that, you can answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am asking you whether you saw them shoot at anyone.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Not only once but many times. I saw it with my own eyes. And to go from one house to another, you had to go in the shadow of walls, because they were in every nook and cranny, they were firing. Moreover, my house looks over a lane, and in the lower part of this lane there are local Serbs living who were our neighbours until recently, and they were all armed. The Trajkovic family, the Cvetkovic family, and then the Jovanovic family. They were all -- all of them, 16 years and above, they were all armed. I saw them with my own eyes. Until yesterday, we were neighbours. And they were either all armed or with police uniform, camouflage police uniform, and some of them had military uniforms, and some of them even had what we call Chetnik caps with the symbols of the old monarchy. I saw this with my own eyes, because it was only a lane that divides my family from their houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You've explained all of this at great length, but you haven't answered the question. Did you see them kill anyone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's another question. It wasn't the question which you asked before. But still, Mr. Berisha, you can answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I saw them firing. I don't -- when we talk about 26th of March, when the massacre was committed at the craftsman centre in Suhareke, I saw them firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see them kill anyone in Suva Reka? Were you present during such an occurrence?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I wasn't able to be present. Not anybody was able to be present because anybody who's there or anybody who went out on the road, it would have been a catastrophe. You would have been a dead man. For that reason, it was impossible to be that close when people were killed, but those people who were fired on were killed. And we looked after ourselves in our own houses, hiding behind walls. And at any moment, we had to be ready to flee to the river, among the trees by the river. And in --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, I asked you whether you saw them kill anyone. You say that you did not see them do that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I didn't see them killing them, but the people who are now missing were killed by them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You can infer whatever you want. I asked you whether you saw this, and I got an answer. And now you tell me that members of the Kuci and Ramadani family or the family Ramadani Jashari, that the members of that family told you that on the 24th of March, in the centre of town, some people were robbed and killed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I said on the 25th of March, sometime between 6.00 and 6.30. The family of Ramadan Berisha and other families with different surnames on one side of the Prizren-Prishtina road, that is, on the right-hand side, in our yard fled, saying that the Serbian police had killed on the street that goes through the old town and having burned the house of Agim Ramadani. Out of fear, they described how they got up and they didn't have even shoes. They had to flee to the river. And on the 25th of March, sometime round about 6.30, we -- because we are a large family and -- 200 of us in all, most of them were forced on tractors and trailers, were forced to gather their belongings and take shelter by the river on the outskirts of the town because of the fear of the police coming at any moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, in relation to this other occurrence - Kuci, Jashari, et cetera - did you see any of these killings or lootings? Did you see any of that?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I didn't see them because I was on the other side of town. But the people who came to my house, to my yard, they told me that these people were killed, Mevdi Jashari [phoen] and others, on the road of the old town. They told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right. Please, could you try to cut this short, because I don't want to spend this much time on all of this. What are you personally testifying about, Mr. Berisha?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I'm testifying to the massacre of 26th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. That's not for you to say. What's important is the evidence which you give. Now, Mr. Milosevic, what you must ask the witness about is the evidence he's given in his statement. If you want to ask any questions about that, you can do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right. All right, Mr. May. No problem whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far away is the village of Savrove from Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Savrove is on the road, on the main road, about five to six kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And why did you think that you should go to the village?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I have a friend there, and I went because I saw a lot of police forces in Suhareke, in the town, and also to take my family away. Only myself, my wife, and my brother Jashar remained at home. He was manager of the petrol station. And on the 26th of March, he went to work and never came back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. On the 25th of March, as you say, on the 25th of March, your brother was working unhindered at the workplace; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please pause before answering.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that you or your brother were not at the shopping centre where the alleged killing of the Albanians took place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, I'm going to interrupt you. You're being asked by the interpreters if you could leave a break after the question so it can be interpreted, and then answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 26th of March, my brother went to work at the petrol station. At 12.20 -- until 12.20, nothing happened. But at that time, he telephoned me and said at the shopping centre, which is not even five metres from the petrol station, it's adjacent to the petrol station, he said, "All of you leave home because a massacre is taking place at the shopping centre." This was a phone conversation, and it was his suggestion that I should leave. I told him, "What are you waiting for then? Why are you not leaving too?" And he said to me, "I will come home at 5.00, when my work is finished."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Berisha. Let us try to shorten these questions. You phoned a Serb family in order to find out where Jashar was, and then afterwards, you called yet another family, et cetera. Were you on good terms with the Serbs who lived in Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: It's true. It's true that we phoned the family of Milutin Trajkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Their names do not matter. My question was whether you were on good terms with them. Does that mean that throughout this time that you are testifying about, you were communicating with the local Serbs and you personally did not have any problems with them?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: We didn't have any problems. But they replied that, "We know nothing of what's going on." Your Honour, if you allow me to make an explanation. On the 5th of April of this year, my cousin -- this same Milutin Trajkovic, who is now in Serbia, telephoned my cousin and said why my relatives were killed between five and six by the department store in Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, please, what was that? Trajkovic asked your cousin, right?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Telephoned from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, in Suva Reka and in the surrounding area on the 25th of March, on the 26th, and the 27th, and on the 28th - that is to say we are talking about the period between the 25th and the 28th - was there any fighting there?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: There was no fighting in the town of Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you say that you heard a loud explosion and you saw the minaret on the mosque blown up; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. On the 28th of March, 1999, sometime at around 11.55, we heard a great explosion. And when we watched -- looked at the minaret, which is about 300 metres away, we saw that the minaret had gone. Meanwhile, in that five or six minutes period, on the road that leads towards Prishtina, we saw a Gazik [phoen] vehicle, a camouflaged vehicle going towards Birac, which is three kilometres from Suhareke, where army forces were stationed. And we saw that the minaret of the mosque in Suhareke had been destroyed. That was the Bajram holiday, which is a festival for Albanian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, was anybody killed in that mosque?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: No. Fortunately, nobody was inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, do Muslims go to the mosque on the holiday of Bajram?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: We go to the mosque. But nobody went on this day because we knew what would happen if we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did not go to the mosque even on Bajram because you knew that somebody would target the mosque. Mr. Berisha --

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. We didn't go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was a KLA sniper perhaps on the minaret? Is that perhaps the reason why you didn't go to the mosque? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please. You've sworn to tell the truth here.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: The KLA was never in Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were president of the municipality, a public figure, a politician, very well-informed. You don't know anything about KLA activities in the territory of Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: KLA activities were never in the town. They were in the outskirts, only in the outskirts, among the villagers. In the hills and mountains, the KLA was active there. And that is where fighting took place. There was fighting in the village of Sllapuzhan, in the village of Semetishti, in Doberdolan and so forth, but there was no fighting in the towns. There was no possibility of them being there because of the large number of police forces and military forces. They were -- they were in Damper and on the pass of Dules, because the army only used to pass through Suhareke, travelling between Prizren and the pass of Dules.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know how many Albanians in the territory of Suva Reka were killed by the KLA during 1998 and until the beginning of the war in 1999? Do you know how many Albanians the KLA killed in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know of any who were killed. I don't know at all. There were people killed on the front in the war, with the Serbs, with the Serb police and military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am not talking about that. I am talking about Albanians that the KLA killed on the territory of our municipality. You know nothing about that?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I don't know what you're talking about, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, for example, I have a list here of Albanians who were killed by the KLA in your municipality. I don't know whether you know any of these people: Bajraktari Xhavit, Bytyqi Petric [phoen], Gashi Bexhet, Gashi Umat [phoen], Gashi Uzdija, Gashi Hajria, Kallolli Latif, Kallolli Lusha, Kryeziu Xhemajl or Xhemal, Kryeziu Sadri, Rokla Sulejman [phoen], Kafaj Xhemajl, Kafaj Ibrahim, Kafaj Ismail, Kafaj Riza, Here Sajapas [phoen]. Do you know any one of these names of people who were killed in the territory of your municipality by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I know that Sadri Kryeziu was killed near a newspaper kiosk. There was an attack, an assassination. Misko, who was the head of the state secret police in Suhareke, by him. He was killed on -- inside, because I heard about that, inside a shop. And Petric Gashi [phoen], was killed on the street -- on the road to Rreshtan. The others, I don't know about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you do know about some crimes that were committed in Suva Reka by the KLA. You've just mentioned three of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He did not say they were committed by the KLA. That is what you said. He merely said that he knew the deaths of people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said they were killed. I didn't say who killed them. I don't know who killed them. There was never a proper investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, as a person who is familiar with the situation in Suva Reka, what do you think? Who killed these people whose names I read out to you, people who were activists and officials, loyal citizens, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He has said that he doesn't know who killed them. So there's no point going on about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you sure you don't know that the KLA killed them? Even the assassination that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: That's the job of the judiciary and the authorities to find out who killed them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know -- I mean, I was referring to Albanians now because you're Albanian, but do you know how many Serbs were killed in the territory of the municipality of Suva Reka? Bogdan Lazic in Suva Reka itself, on the 23rd of March, for example? On the 23rd of March, three or four days before what you've been testifying about. Then Zoran Mihajlovic, Radovan Mihajlovic. All right, this was in Musutiste but all of that is Suva Reka, but then this one was in Suva Reka. Do you know about these killings?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I know on the 23rd of March Lazic was killed in a shop there, but I know it was -- there were ten Albanians were killed by vendetta on a street behind the post office. There was one woman and eight men and still their bodies have still not been found. But it was a question of vendetta, of blood feuding. They were in -- a question of retaliation, rather. The police killed eight people, eight Albanians on the 23rd of March. There was one woman and the rest were men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, please, how come you know that? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... see them. My house is quite a ways away, but I heard about it. And they still don't know where the bodies are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know about who carried out the assassination, and you say that it is for the judiciary to give their say. And as for these Albanians that you did not see, you say that it was the police who killed them. You know who did that.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, because --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you didn't see that either, right?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: The relatives of the people who were killed saw the police shooting at their -- at their relatives. But they live quite a ways away from where I live. And they said that the police entered the houses and killed the people in retaliation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right, Mr. Berisha. Anyway, do you know how many soldiers were killed in the territory of the municipality of Suva Reka, how many policemen were killed in the territory of the municipality of Suva Reka? Do you know anything about that, Mr. Berisha?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nothing? All right. Let's continue. So on Bajram, there was no one at the mosque. No one was killed when the minaret was blown up. And you say that they did not go to the mosque because they knew what would happen. And you reject that it was the KLA that was on the minaret, that their sniper was on the minaret and that they would not be crazy enough to go there and risk losing their lives?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No need to go into an argument about that. He's dealt with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You claim that a Serb policeman warned you to escape to Albania, allegedly because of the danger of paramilitary forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: On the 28th of March, 1999, around 5.00 in the afternoon, maybe 5.20, I didn't -- don't remember the name of the policeman, but I think -- now I remember. It's Nojic Djura, a local policeman, was -- came into my courtyard. Nojic Djura. I didn't remember at the time when I made the statement. He said to me, "You have to make -- get yourselves ready within 15 minutes, because they might come. The army and the police will come and are going to kill you all. So get ready and go to Albania." This was on the 28th of March, 1999. So I had my family in Savrove, and my wife and I -- my brother was still at the gas station, so my wife and I went on foot to Savrove to find the rest of them. And the other members of my family had to get ready as well as they could, with their tractors and cars, and set off for Albania. On that day, there was a -- there were a lot of people from Suhareke leaving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, was the policeman your neighbour at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, he was. But he was wearing camouflage -- a camouflage uniform at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was the atmosphere like when he told you to leave the village? Was it like a threat to you or was it a kind of some friendly advice being concerned with the safety of your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He said literally, "Go to Albania, because others are going to come." We didn't ask who the others would be. And they were -- "They're going to slit your throats." Those were his words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, you said just now he said, "Go to Albania because others would come."

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you did not even ask him who these others were; is that right? And in the statement, you say that he said to you the paramilitary formations would come, et cetera, et cetera. So as for the paramilitary formations, that was your conclusion or you just invented that? Because now you say that he said others would come, and you did not even ask him who these others would be. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: We knew who they would be. They were police from Serbia and soldiers coming from Serbia. We knew that. There was no reason to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's now time for the break. Mr. Milosevic, you've had your three-quarters of an hour, but in view of the documents which have been put in, which apparently had been disclosed earlier, but in view of that, we will give you, if you want, some more time ask some questions about them. Do you want to ask some questions about these documents or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps only a few. But not only about the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've had your three-quarters of an hour. You can ask some questions about the documents, though, because it's right that you should have time to do so. You can look at them during the break. Ms. Romano, these documents have been put in in a totally unsatisfactory state, I have to say. If documents are to be put before a Court, they must be done in order. They must have a list attached to them. They must be stapled together. They must be put in a workmanlike form before the Court. And I have to tell you that if it's not done that way, then the Trial Chamber will be minded to reject them, because we simply can't get on with documents which just come in a pile to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honours, these documents were not treated as exhibits. They were treated as an attachment to the statement. That is the form that was provided and disclosed, so that was the form we used. But we're happy to just form a binder or anything else that can help the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Berisha, we're going to adjourn now. Would you be back in 20 minutes to conclude your evidence. Would you remember meanwhile not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include members of the Prosecution. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic, is there anything you want to ask about these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is, but before I do that, I have a couple of question which I think are important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They will take perhaps one minute or two, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 4, paragraph 4, you state that your son, together with another six young men was arrested on the 16th of May. Were your son or his friends abused, beaten, or mistreated in any way?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: On the 15th of May, 1999, in my uncle's house, my son Luan and eight others, my cousins, were present. And several policemen came and said, "What are you doing here?" And then they came and -- and came -- there came a summons from Misko, who is head of the secret police in Suhareke, and they didn't mistreat them but told them on the next day, 16th of May, at noon, to come to the municipality. And they asked my son where your father is, and they told him to come to the municipality the next day. To turn up at 12.00 the next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But if I understood you correctly, precisely that person, Misko Nisavic, whom you mentioned a moment ago, after you came to the municipal building at his request which he conveyed through your son, that man apologised after your ten-minute discussion that he had to invite you to the police station. Did he or any of his colleagues mistreat you?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: On the next day, 16th of May, I and eight others went in front of the municipality building and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, could you just concentrate on the question. The question was were you mistreated? Perhaps you could just answer that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we were not mistreated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now about these documents. You said that you had found a floppy disk of some kind, including names and personal details of soldiers, units they belonged to. You found that in the municipal building, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: The material was presented to me in the name of -- about the soldiers. It was brought by some citizens who found it in a computer, and it shows the names, surnames of Serbian soldiers who were in Suhareke region. There were about 600, 700 of them. And I have submitted it because it shows the number of soldiers as they themselves describe themselves present in my municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That means that all these papers originate from that floppy disk; right? I just wish to say one thing. I checked with my associate, Mr. Ognjenovic; we hadn't received this heap of paper before, but I don't think it's very important in any case, because what we're dealing here, in fact, with are lists of conscripts, then members of staffs of civilian defence by municipalities. Do you believe this to be important for your testimony, Mr. Berisha? What is the significance of these documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, I've told you before, it's not for the witness to say. It's a matter for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I consider --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that case, I also see here an Official Gazette designating electoral units for the elections. It's blurred, but it must be 1990, 1991, or 1992. I also see conclusions about some schools. But most of these papers are lists and records containing first, last names, fathers' names, dates, addresses, telephone numbers of conscripts. Then we have a record of motor vehicles, indicating their licence plates, then some commendations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, have you got any questions? We can see that. It may be you are right in what you say about the significance of these documents, but that's going to be a matter we will have to determine in due course. Now, we've got the witness here. You've got another two or three questions. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right. No problem, Mr. May. I have just one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what lies the importance of these papers, Mr. Berisha, in your mind? Supplies and materiel, fuel, et cetera, what does this have to do with your testimony?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I consider that these are rather important documents. First of all, regarding the number of delegates at the Assembly of the municipality, you can see that they were all the names of Serbs, even though the proportion of the population in the municipality were 95 per cent Albanians to 5 per cent Serbs, which shows that this Assembly had no kind of legitimacy to decide in the name of Albanian citizens. That's the significance of the documents I brought. The second document in the Official Gazette, you can see the cultural genocide --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, I'm afraid we haven't got time to go through all these documents, and with respect, it's going to be a matter for us to decide the significance of them in the context of this trial against this accused. Now, Mr. Tapuskovic, have you got any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have just a couple of questions for Mr. Berisha. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Berisha, before the 24th of March in 1998 and until the 24th of March, did you know of any conflicts all over Kosovo between the KLA and the Serb army and the police, especially in Drenica?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: We were informed by the press and the media that there had been clashes between the KLA and the Serbian army in Drenica, but only through the press because travelling from -- to Prishtina and Prizren was very difficult. So in November, after 1996, I didn't travel either to Prizren or to Prishtina because of the danger on the roads and the police patrols, and especially the checkpoint at Lubisht on the Suhareke-Prizren road and the checkpoint of the Serbian police forces at Saraljeva on the Suhareke-Prishtina road, so I never travelled after 1996. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, what I'm interested in is the following: Due to these clashes that indeed existed, in your area where there were no clashes, did people from those areas which were afflicted come to your municipality to find shelter?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: There were only isolated cases in our municipality. There were not many, and mainly they took refuge in the villages round Suhareke, not in the city. That is, before July 1998 -- June 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But for the most part, people migrated within the territory of Kosovo to find cover and shelter.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another thing I want to ask has to do with something you said in your statement. You said at one point you found yourself in the village of Buzhalle; is that correct? And at that moment in that house where you spent a couple of days, there were about 130 people. That was in the beginning of April.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: This was from 29th March, 1999, until 3 -- 3rd of April. There were 130 of us living in this house in Buzhalle. That was my family, the family of my in-laws in Savrove, and family from Semetish and local people from the house where we were staying. We were all together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the night, did you go to the basement?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: This house didn't have a basement. It was a normal house. But it merely had some woods nearby.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can understand that. But after that, you continued to say that you went to Prizren, then you stayed with your aunt, and you left Kosovo sometime after the 21st of May; is that correct? Well, in this regard, I would like to know the following: Do you know that the NATO bombed Kosovo, among other areas, that bombs fell in Kosovo too?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: On the 3rd of April, my two sons and I didn't go to Prizren, but it was my brother, Afrim, and we took shelter in the woods. After two days they returned to Prizren because the police sent them back. And Luan and Shyqet, my two sons and I, stayed in the mountains. And during that time, we heard explosions during the night, and we don't know where these bombs of NATO forces were falling because we didn't have any information. We didn't have any television or radio, we just heard these explosions during the night. And when they were closer, the explosions were closer and when they were further off, they were fainter. But we didn't know where they were falling. And then until the night of 30th April to 1st of May, I was in the woods. And then I came down to Suhareke, to my aunt's house, Hajrie Gashi, and stayed there until the 21st of May. On 21st of May at 10 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's deal with this. Mr. Tapuskovic, do you have any other questions you want to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I only wanted to know in this regard whether he knew that there were victims both among Albanians and Serbs and whether those bombs created fear among them. That's all I wanted to know. Was he afraid that he could be killed himself?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: There were no -- there was nobody killed by NATO bombs in Suhareke, in the town, and the Albanian population was not at all frightened of the NATO bombing. And I was there until 21st of May, and then I was deported to Albania. On that day, there were about 5.000 people deported from Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wladimiroff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If the Court will allow me, I have a few questions related to the documents, just to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think our rule was only one amicus --

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I realize that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
