utterances.text: -- but as an exception, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I'm very grateful. Questioned by Mr. Wladimiroff:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you told the Court you did not find the floppy disk yourself; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I just got the material.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who gave it to you? Could you give us a name?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: A citizen brought it to my office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you prepared to --

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: And it was photocopied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring to the floppy disk, so I take it that that was not photocopied, was it?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: No, no. It was copied from the computer. And I received the material, I didn't get the disk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So you did not print it yourself.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. I've got a few questions about the documents which were not from the floppy disk. Did you find these documents yourself?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I found the other documents in the office where I'd worked from the 8th of October, 1990 to -- up to the 30th of October, 2000, when I was deputy chief of the board. I found the material in the office. Whereas the first documents were given to me -- were handed over to me when I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. You made a documentation list, which you handed over to the Prosecution, that lists all the documents you found; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is one document in this pile which is not listed? That's a decision to appoint managerial organs in the Jovanovic Zmaj Cultural Institute of Suva Reka. Is that one of the documents you found or is that document mistakenly in the pile?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I don't know, but normally all the documents there were found in my office, except for the first, which we mentioned, which were given to me in the office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will show you a document very quickly, and if you can tell the Court whether that's one of the documents you found in your office, because it's not on your list.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: May I ask the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I found in the office when I went back to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It is in the pile, Your Honours, after number 9, but it is not listed, just to clarify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've got a question related to document number 3 in your pile, and again I will quickly ask the usher to show it to you.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: This is a list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you say this is a list of armed Serbs of the Unit of Gypsy Slayers. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say so? Because the document does not indicate anything of that kind.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: The people in the list are all local Serbs from the villages, from the various villages. They wrote that themselves, Romi Koljaci. That's Gypsy Slayers. I didn't write it myself. It was a photocopy for -- about the Commander Sinisic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand what you say, but where do you see on the document that this is related to the Unit of Gypsy Slayers?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: On the other side. On the other part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: With their -- in their writing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And then I've got a question about document number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: May I ask the usher again to show it to the witness, please. The second page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: No. This is their handwriting about the massacre in the village of Trnje on the 25th of May in 1999 when a lot of people were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can read that.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: They wrote it. They wrote it in Cyrillic script.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You assume that Serbs wrote it?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Thank you. Now I've got a question about the photograph. That's number 5 off the list.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: This is a person from Reshane, the village of Reshane.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Do not answer things I did not ask you. Whose handwriting is that? Would you know that?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: It's the person -- the handwriting of the person in question in Cyrillic there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person in question is the person on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: On the other side, the back of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. But it's on the back of -- it was written on the back of the photograph. It's that person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's clarified. Thank you very much. And then I've got a final question about number 13. Do you know whose handwriting this is?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I found this in the office where I was working, where the head of the board, Stanislav Andjelkovic, had been working. That's his handwriting. I recognise his handwriting. And there's also a number of his -- of my, rather -- my telephone number is at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take this page out of a bundle of pages or was it just that page you found on his desk?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: No. I took it out of the calendar. And it's my writing in the corner there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's all I ask, Your Honours, just to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Romano.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't have any further questions for the witness. I just have one clarification about the disclosure. The statement in English was disclosed on the 25th of January, 2002, and the B/C/S on 15 April, and the attachments, both in English and B/C/S, on the 22nd of May. So the accused had them before. And I think it's highlighted also by Mr. Wladimiroff. In the statement there is the list of all the documents in the pile. I know that, unfortunately, that was not provided in accordance of your satisfactory, but I think it's -- at least you have the list in the statement. And again, I just highlight the fact that these documents are attachment to the statement and in order to complete the statement provided by the witness and by the facts that he related upon discrimination and the removal of his position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So you're not seeking to have them exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No. I seek to have them exhibited as part of the statement in order to clarify and complement the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's a distinction, if I may say, without a difference. I mean, either they're going to be exhibited or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No. The request is to be exhibited, and the relevance is up to the Court to give it later on. But I just want to clarify that they complement the statement of the accused and the -- not the accused, sorry, the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. They will be part of Exhibit 240, if I recollect rightly. Yes. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, let's go back to the 26th of March, 1999. In your statement, you wrote that around 2.30 in the afternoon, you went to the Gashi family neighbourhood, and you rang your brother Jashar, and you heard from Jashar that Jashar had heard that -- he heard that some -- shooting, exploding, and people screaming from the shopping centre and that Sedat, Nexhat, and Bujar had died there. Is it right? Do you know if there were any survivors from the scene?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. There were two women, Vjollca and Gramozi, a son, and Shyhrete Berisha, who survived the massacre. Vjollca, Gramozi and the third one, Shyhrete Berisha. They survived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you know where they are, the survivors, at this point?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Vjollca and Gramozi in Suhareke. She works in a factory and Gramozi is in school. I visited them at home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the corpses of the bodies who died there?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: We do know now that they're in a mass grave in Belgrade, and we're waiting for the UNMIK authorities in Prishtina to request that the Serb authorities return the bodies. They were -- according to the newspapers, they were in mass graves in blankets. We found that out from the Prishtina office, that during the exhumation of bodies in Belgrade, some documents of family members, of my family members were found there. And Lirije Berisha in particular, who was pregnant, she was in the eighth month of pregnancy, her body was recognised because of the baby in her body. And we're asking the authorities, the UNMIK authorities in Prishtina, to do what they can to get the bodies returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berisha. And I have a point to raise to the Prosecution. My understanding is that this witness, Mr. Berisha, was brought to give evidence regarding the indictment, 66[D] or Schedule K in the Suva Reka killing, and I heard that there are some survivors.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's specific for the facts that happened in the coffee shop in the Suva Reka event. The proper witness would be Shyhrete Berisha who will testify, I think, probably next week. And he gave evidence but more hearsay evidence. Specifically, that fact and the killings that occurred in the coffee shop, we have the witness next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: We have the other witness, who is Hysni Berisha. Your Honours, while we wait for the witness. If I may address the Court also in order to not get any problems in the future, we have attachments to the statement again, and they are three attachments. They consist a map, a list, and a sketch. And I will just go, with the witness, while I will be making the summary, because we have also photos in the Suva Reka binder that you will be able to address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If there are a few attachments, it's not a difficulty. It's if there are a large pile, as we had in the last one.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I'm afraid it's a little bit big because the list is extensive, but they are in fact three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat. Examined by Ms. Romano:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, can you please state your full name to the Court.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. My name is Hysni Sylejman Berisha.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, were you born on 12 April 1948, in Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I'm a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, you provided a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 20 August of 2001; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on 13 March 2002, in Suva Reka, you attended a meeting with a representative of the Registrar, and you were informed about the contents of your statement. You had your statement read out to you, and you had the opportunity to review it and to ascertain if the contents that the written statement were true; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also made an addendum to your statement?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The Prosecution submits the statement and attachments into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 241 for the original and 241A for the redacted version.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The witness is currently the chairman of the Association for Missing Persons and Victims of War in Suva Reka. He describes the events in Suva Reka after the OSCE evacuated on 20 March 1999. He heard gunfire and could see flames coming from houses near the technical school on Restane road. On the morning of the 26 March 1999, Serb forces started to shell around Suva Reka, using tanks and Pragas. The witness saw many police moving towards a house across from the police station. About two to three hours later, he heard shooting from the police station in the vicinity of Sedat Berisha's house and saw smoke and flames coming from that direction. The following day, on seeing the police continue to torch buildings, the witness took his family to the home of a neighbour where there were 10 [sic] to 100 people sheltering in the basement. They left and went to a field where they were soon surrounded by paramilitaries who Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. demanded money and valuables from them. One of these paramilitaries grabbed the witness's daughter and threatened to shoot her unless the witness handed money over. The commander intervened and released the witness's child, telling the witness, "Go to Albania." The witness set off in convoy. On the 15th of April they were again robbed by paramilitaries, of approximately 4.000 Deutschmarks before being allowed to continue on to Prizren. En route, a number of civilians were wounded and killed by Serb forces. On the outskirts of Prizren, the convoy was told to return to their place of origin. Upon his return to Suva Reka on or about the 6th April, the witness saw buildings burning and found that his home had been looted. Over the ensuing days, he observed numerous Serb forces in military jeeps and stolen vehicles around the town. They were looting shops and homes. On the 12th May, the witness observed a column of approximately 50.000 civilians pass through Suva Reka. He spoke with some of them and was told that there had been a Serb offensive in the village of Budakove. They had been ordered by paramilitaries to go to Albania. The witness remained in Suva Reka until 21st May, 1999 when he was again ordered by Serb forces to leave Kosovo. The witness names those responsible as paramilitary and local police. He went to Prizren and stayed at a relative's home until KFOR arrived. The witness followed KFOR into Suva Reka on the 13 June 1999. Thereafter, the witness assisted the British forensic team and undertook an investigation into the Berisha family massacre and the events at the coffee shop on the 26 March 1999. He describes the location of the items of clothing and artefacts at the murder scenes, victims' homes, and at the cemetery. He produces a number of documents in relation to his investigation. The witness gives a breakdown of the numbers of persons killed and missing in the Suva Reka municipality and the number and type of buildings destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, attached to your statement there is a map and there is a list of names of missing people. Did you do the list? Did you produce this list?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. I drew it up. The list and the map of the graves.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can I please have the usher show the witness the drawing of the graves. And I also need the witness to be shown the Suva Reka binder. I believe it's Exhibit number 166, tab 3. In the tab 3. I think I open here, maybe it's easier for you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tab 3 are photos K0141454 on. Mr. Berisha, can you explain first what the sketch is? Your sketch, Mr. Berisha.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The usher, can you please put first the sketch, the sketch that the witness has. Yes. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just very briefly explain to the Court what is this sketch? What did you draw in this sketch?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: This sketch shows one of the four graveyards in Suhareke created after the war. This is according to the -- the code is number 1, the grave of the Berisha family, as buried by the Serbian forces. These were people massacred in the massacre of 25th of March --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha --

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: -- in Suhareke and other villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Berisha, that photo -- the usher can please put the photo -- is exactly what you tried to draw in your sketch?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters request the witness to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is photograph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you speak into the microphone, please. I know it's difficult to look at it, but could you please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the same thing and I did it in the sketch form, in the simple form myself. This is the Suhareke-Rreshtan-Pecan crossroads. These are the Berisha family graves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honours, also in relation to the statement and the witness also, the facts that the witness is able to testify relate to the identification of the clothing and some artefacts from the victims of Suva Reka while he was in the -- following the British forensic team. And they are reflected in the Suva Reka binder, in tabs 3 that are the photos, tabs 4 and 5. I -- unless the Court wants, I don't think we need to show the witness them. Thank you, Mr. Berisha. And that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The photograph can come back. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it correct here where your details are provided that you were a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I was not -- I was not a lawyer but in translation from Albanian into English it has come out like that. I was a legal officer in a construction enterprise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do as a legal officer in a construction company?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I was an administrative worker.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can one infer, therefore, that in terms of schooling or experience you have no experience whatsoever in investigations related to the commission of crimes and similar investigations?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I'm not a judicial expert, and I haven't gone into this question professionally, but I've gone into these questions from a humanitarian point of view, and I have submitted to the Court material for -- to aid their prosecution and about your staff that worked in Suhareke municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In your statement, you say that from the 13th of June, you started -- onwards, you started with investigations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: It's true. On the 13th of June, after the NATO troops entered, I started investigating the graves of my family, the Berishas, and of others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in which field or, rather, in which area did you carry out your investigations, only in Orahovac or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: First of all, I investigated, as I said before, the fate of my own relatives, and later the need arose to investigate further cases in the municipality of Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And how did you investigate? Did you observe things directly or by way of collecting some kind of evidence or in some other way? How did you investigate?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: First we started investigations by examining the houses where massacres were committed, and there we found evidence of crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in connection with which incidents and which events did you carry out investigations, except for what you said at the beginning with regard to your family, that is?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I conducted investigations of all the massacres that took place in Suhareke municipality from 22nd of March to the 2nd of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you dealing with all events, if I understood you correctly? You said all of them, or were you dealing with Albanians only? If you dealt with everything, then did you deal with the non-Albanian population that were victims as well?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I said that I based my investigations on the massacres committed between 26th of March and the 6th of June, 1999. And I didn't go into incidents that took place after the 13th of June because KFOR were there and they were able to look into these things under their responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But as for the periods that you dealt with, with all these events, these criminal offences that you investigated, it is certain that there were also non-Albanian victims. Have you dealt with a single non-Albanian victim?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: As for identifying missing persons, this process is still continuing. We are still investigating these matters. And all cases that are submitted to the association for the investigation of missing persons are looked into. We look into all these cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, I asked you about what you said in your answer to the previous question, that you dealt with all events in that period that you mentioned. When you say "all," that presupposes everybody, not only Albanians, and I asked you whether you had a single example of having dealt with a victim who was not Albanian. Just tell me yes or no.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: There were no non-Albanian victims. I don't know of a single case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You say that you were observing the Serb forces moving in your town in order to inform people around you. Is that correct? That's on page number 2, in paragraph number 2 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Could you ask that question again, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you were observing Serb forces as they were moving in your town so that you could inform the people who lived around you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who are these people that you informed?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: The defenseless civilian population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they the same thing that you were? Were they the same as you?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. I was one of these civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that they themselves could not see where the Serb forces were moving?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: People who saw these things made their own observations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that the OSCE was stationed across the street from the Secretariat of the Interior in Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Not exactly opposite.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did the OSCE function normally in Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am asking whether the OSCE normally functioned in Suva Reka, whether they were carrying out their tasks, performing the functions for which they were there. It was you who observed everything?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: In the period that I was discussing, there were no OSCE people in Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But you lived in Suva Reka. And I'm asking you about the OSCE in Suva Reka, before they withdrew, that is to say until the 20th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: The OSCE did not withdraw on the 20th of March but on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You say that on the 26th of March, at 8.00, the shelling of Suva Reka started. Until then, it had been peaceful. And you say that the OSCE was there until the 18th. Now, please answer the following question: Do you know anything about any crimes committed by the KLA in 1998 and 1999 in the area of Suva Reka until that 26th of March?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Perhaps you haven't understood my statement properly, because my description starts on the 26th of March, the first massacre at 6.30 in the morning when the Serbian forces killed 36 civilians, and then in the second massacre in which 48 members of the Berisha family were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You do say, though, that on the 26th of March at 8.00, the shelling of Suva Reka started. That's page 2, paragraph 4. You say that this was a usual occurrence which had been going on since August 1998. That's what you said. So on the basis of that, one can infer what I've been asking you about. Are you claiming that Suva Reka was shelled while the OSCE was still there? Because I never found that in the OSCE reports, so I'm surprised, and I would like you to clarify the situation for me.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: It's not true that Suhareke was shelled, either in 1998 or 1999. There were positions in various villages that were shelled from Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean "shelled from Suva Reka"?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Suhareke was under a steel siege, and there were Serbian military forces stationed in -- around Suhareke in the place known as Birac, in Damper, and in the vineyards. They -- there was heavy military equipment stationed there in the vineyards, and this was used to shell --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, that's not what I'm asking you. I wanted to clarify what you wrote here in your statement. You said that on the -- this is the penultimate paragraph on the first page of the statement, which is actually number 2 because first is the page with your details. And then it says: "The following morning on the 26th of March, 1999 about 8.00 a.m. in the morning, the Serbs commenced to shell around Suva Reka from the hill behind the township." Full stop. "This was a usual occurrence which had been going on since August 1998." Full stop. So you say that on the 26th of March, the shelling started and this was a usual thing because it had been going on since August 1998. And I asked you does that mean that even while the OSCE was there - and they were there from October until March 1999 - and I didn't find anything about this shelling in any one of the OSCE reports so I'm asking you whether it is your claim that from August 1998 onwards the shelling of Suva Reka was a usual occurrence, as you put in your statement. I just quoted your statement to you so could you please explain that.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: It's not true what you say. The truth is that these positions, Yugoslav army positions, were used to shell the villages from these positions around Suhareke. I didn't say that Suhareke itself was shelled. A part of Suhareke was burned in July 1998 by Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I won't comment on the fact that in not a single OSCE report is this shelling mentioned. But let's come back to the first paragraph on page 3. You said that on the 21st of March -- 28th of March 1999, you left the basement where you had hidden with your family. Why did you go to that basement in the first place? You and 70 or 100 other people which you say -- who you say were in the basement with you. Why did you take cover there?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I described how on 26th of March, how the massacre of the Berisha family took place. On the 27th, the police started burning the houses in the part of town where the massacre took place, and they reached my house where I was with my family and some neighbours. And we thought that they would come to us, so we decided to go to a basement to protect ourselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But you say on page 3 of your statement -- you explain how the Serbs always went in to attack in the morning, and you went into the basement in the evening. Were you perhaps taking cover from NATO bombing in that basement, Mr. Berisha?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I know that you're trying to get -- get away the truth, but I am saying that every morning the shelling started in the direction of the villages. This was an operation against the civilian population. You yourself know how you organised it. This wasn't the -- it wasn't the reason that we went to the cellar because we were scared of NATO. NATO never bombed Suhareke. Nor were we ever afraid of NATO attacks. They were our rescuers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do you know that at least 5.000 tonnes of bombs were dropped on Kosovo? Do you really think that no one could have been killed by them, by those saviour bombs of which there were 500 -- 5.000 tonnes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is all a matter of argument.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then tell me, if you were not taking cover -- you said a moment ago that Serbs shelled from Suva Reka the villages around Suva Reka, and I understood that you said they were shelling Suva Reka. What is it exactly that you claim; that they shelled Suva Reka or that they shelled villages around Suva Reka from Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He has made that quite plain. He has said they did not shell Suva Reka itself but shelling the villages around. That's what you asked him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was a question that referred to 1998, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When you're asking him, which day are you asking about now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 26th of March. The period from the 26th of March. That's what we're talking about now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Can you deal with that, Mr. Berisha? Were they shelling at Suva Reka itself or were they shelling the villages, from the 26th of March?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. The shelling continued from the same positions where Serbian forces had been stationed. These were military and police forces. The shelling of the villages never stopped in 1999. It -- but in the town of Suhareke, it wasn't shelling, it was an infantry offensive in March 1999 where they came into houses and killed innocent civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right. We have clarified that. Since you claim that you were not hiding from bombs in that basement, does that mean that when the police were attacking you, as you say, you were inside houses targeted by the police, and when the police withdrew during the night, you were in shelters? Is that a fact that I am supposed to infer from your testimony?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: The truth is that we took shelter in the cellar because of our insecurity. Because at 1.00 in the morning, on the basis of the fact that most police operations took place in the early hours of the morning, I and others had to flee from the cellar and take refuge in -- elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. From that shelter you went to a house about one and a half kilometres away; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I'm not sure exactly how far it was, but we did go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And whose house was that, and how did you happen to go there? Why did you decide to go there? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: We decided to go there, as I explained, for safety. And the house belonged to my cousin Idriz Berisha.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many of you were there and who was there with you?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Three families went. That is my own, my brother's, and my cousin's. I mean with our families.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You state that members of paramilitary units arrived on the 3rd of April, 1999. They reached that house. They had AK-47 automatic rifles; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: The truth is that on 3rd of April, 1999, at about 9.00 in the morning, the Serbian police started a lightning offensive in Suhareke. I saw them arriving, burning houses from the western end of Suhareke towards the north, where I was sheltering. And towards the afternoon, they were advancing, always burning houses and firing guns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also say that they had AK-47 automatic rifles; is that right? That's what's written in your description.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I'm not a weapons expert, but I know that they were armed. They had -- they carried firearms and also knives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And not being an expert, why do you claim they were armed with AK-47s?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I saw their automatic rifles myself because they were pointed against me and at my daughter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you know that those were AK-47 automatic rifles?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that AK-47 is the principal weapon of the KLA and not the army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Perhaps it was, but maybe it wasn't as you think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that in all OSCE reports the -- this rifle is described as the weapon of choice for the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's dealt with that. You don't have to answer again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And do you know --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because he was involved and carried out investigations. He told me himself, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Suva Reka was one of the main channels for the transport of weapons from Albania and precisely this type of weapon, AK-47, was brought in from Albania in enormous quantities, especially after the crisis in Albania, looting of warehouses belonging to the army, et cetera? Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I described the case that happened to me and other things that were happening at that time. The Serbian army and police came in police camouflage uniforms, and they had on their arms the red, white, and blue flag. And they threatened us with guns. They took my daughter out of a car and stood her up against a wall and, with the same guns, they also threatened me. I'm talking about a specific incident. I'm not conducting an analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know anything about the transport of weapons by the KLA from Albania?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I know nothing about this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, you've just said that they had armbands on their arms; red, white, and blue. Do you know that red, white, and blue is the Croatian flag, whereas red, blue and white is the Serbian flag?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll adjourn, the lights having gone out,. Mr. Berisha, would you be back in 20 minutes, please. Don't speak to anybody about your evidence meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm at your disposal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us continue where we left off. Of course I'm not suggesting that those were Croats. What I'm suggesting is that since you described them wrongly as far as the Yugoslav flag is concerned, I'm suggesting that you simply didn't know enough to tell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What are you suggesting is wrong with his description? You must put it to him in terms so that he can understand it. What was the armband you say these troops would have worn?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The armband he described was red, white, and blue. Those are the colours of the flags of all Yugoslav peoples, but red, white, and blue is the Croatian colour, whereas red, blue, and white is the Serbian flag. Since he claims he saw it, if he had really seen it, he would have said red, blue, and white. But since he didn't see it, in actual fact, then he confused the colours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: By no means is it easy to understand what distinction you're making. Now, he's described what he saw. Can you say what order these colours were on the armband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I see the accused is trying to turn things upside-down. It's not true. Or maybe it's an interpretation problem, or maybe it's mine. I didn't say what he says I said. I said that they were red and white, whereas -- and blue was the uniform, was the colour of the uniform. Whereas I don't think the details of the colours are that important. But they had tattoos with -- with -- on their arms with the four Cs of the Serb sign, the CCCC on their arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You had uniforms but you saw that they had tattoos on their arms.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I said several times what they were like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those people you speak about, were they in fact members of the KLA involved in battles in Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: There was no UCK, no KLA, in Suhareke. There was Serb police and police from Serbia. Because in my statement I said I saw them, and I said that they had -- I saw them. They had come from Serbia. They were police from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you know that too, that the police had come from outside Kosovo, the police that you saw?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: The person who presented himself as commander said, "We are from Serbia."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he introduce himself to you?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. I had communicated. I talked to him when they threatened to execute my daughter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the same page, you say that those people ordered you to leave Kosovo. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Once they stole our valuables, our money, they ordered us to take off for Albania.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know about the order of the KLA that people should leave Kosovo and go to Macedonia and Albania?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about such an order. But I know that the Serb police threw us out of our homes and out of the country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But you go on to say, and I'm following up on what you said, that the commander of the police, Milan Sipka, stopped you while you were passing by the Progress factory and told you to go back home because the border was sealed off; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: When we were being held hostage, all of us in the column of people near the village of Korice, two days later we were ordered to carry on to Albania. On the way, just on the outskirts of Prizren near the pharmaceutical factory Farmakos, they forced us to go back. The order was given by Milan Sipka, who had earlier been police chief in Suhareke. At that time, he was a high police official in Prizren.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Am I right in understanding you as follows: If the police is not preventing you from going wherever you want - Macedonia, Albania, it doesn't matter - they are then driving you out? And if they tell you to stay at home, then they are keeping you hostage. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't follow the point. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. It's not a clear question. What is the question, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the witness has explained that they were turned back in order to keep them hostage. So if they tell them to go home, that's because they want to keep them hostage. And if they don't stand in their way and let them go wherever they want, he construes that as expulsion. Do you understand now, Mr. May, what kind of wrong description this is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Can you deal with that, Mr. Berisha?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I see that the accused is trying to turn things upside-down here once again. The truth is, and I repeat it once again, on the 3rd of March, the Serb police threw us out of our homes, expelled us and sent us to Albania after having robbed us. On the way, near Malcija e Re, there was a long column of people, several kilometres long, all defenseless civilians near the police station in Lubisht. The police stopped us and wouldn't allow us to continue our journey. There, they held us hostage for two days and two nights, robbing us further and mistreating us further. On the 5th of April, at around 12.00, they ordered us to continue our journey to Albania. We continued, and we got to the outskirts of Prizren near the factory, Farmakos factory, where they returned us back to Suhareke. This is the truth, and this is what the accused is attempting to turn around, to dodge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Please explain this, because you were there: He stopped you. You say the commander of the police, Milan Sipka, stopped you and told you to go home. Did you back to Suva Reka then?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Half the column returned and half stayed where it was. After awhile, the other half was returned, escorted by the police all the time. We returned in the direction of Suhareke, but we were not allowed to turn off the road left or right, go anywhere else. We arrived at Suhareke at about 9.00 in the evening, 21 hours. The department store in Suhareke was near the -- near the department store, there was a police postoblloke control point, and they asked us where we were going. We told them that we had been returned from our journey. One of them, Jovica Popovci, whom I knew, told me, "How can they return you back to your homes when we've expelled you from your homes?" I then told him of the order that Milan Sipka had given us and that that should be checked and if the order is true or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic, you've got five minutes more.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's very little. Too little time, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that the police checked on you regularly from the moment when you came back. Did they do that in order to establish whether the KLA was dropping in on you or whether there were any activities going on or did anyone mistreat you?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: The KLA wasn't active in Suhareke or around the town. As to mistreatment, of course there was mistreatment. We were also robbed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In your statement, you say that you did not obey the order to fill back the trenches dug by the KLA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: The five-member police patrol, among whom was a Sinisa Andrejevic, whom I knew, Petkovic Miki, and a Goran called Ramiz, and a person called Gogic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you just deal with the point, please. Mr. Berisha, could you just deal with the point, because time is short. What's alleged is that you were ordered to fill in trenches, but you didn't. Could you just deal with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The truth is that I didn't fill in the trenches, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were those trenches?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: You know better than I would.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were they dug?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: You would know better, and you would have better information on that than I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Mr. Berisha, I know it may be provoking to have to answer these questions, but they're perfectly proper ones. Now, where were the trenches, please? Can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't go to see them because I didn't take part in the filling up of the trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did the KLA shoot from those trenches at the police? Just say yes or no, please. Time is short. It's flying.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I don't have any information that the KLA ever shot from there, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In your statement, you say that you stayed in Prizren until the 13th of June. Is that correct? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: That's true, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that nobody expelled you from there?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: No, because they didn't know where we were taking refuge at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And is it correct that you went to Prizren to hide from the fighting between the KLA and the army and the police on the other hand? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: No. I went there after the Yugoslav police expelled the whole population of Suhareke on the 21st of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. On page 6, you say that at 1500 hours, when you started all this in the month of June, you started your investigation in places where members of your family were killed. Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. I began investigations there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You further say that you went to the cafe in the northern part of Suva Reka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, where the massacre took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that the cafe had been burnt down and that all the windows were shut and blown away by the explosion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: It was burnt and there were a lot of shells as well as a lot of clothing which was left over from the victims who had been executed there. Cartridges too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how is it possible, since you say that there was an explosion that blasted all the windows, and how come the refrigerator and the heater were unaffected and the cafe was burned down because of this explosion that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: As to the technical details of the fire and why the refrigerator wasn't burnt, I'm sorry, I -- whether it was burnt or not, whether there were traces of the crime or what traces there were, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You say that in that cafe there were many bullet casings and other munitions. Does that mean that somebody was shooting from the room that you were in?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: There was no shooting there. There was an execution. Because it was in the coffee shop. There was shooting, mass shooting, in the coffee shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that means that somebody was shooting from that cafe since there were so many casings in the cafe itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're not talking about bullets, you're talking about casings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Or shooting in the cafe.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the Yugoslav police. You were their commander. All the Berisha family was in there, 48 members, of which 18 children and old people and women. They were all forced into there, that cafe, and they were executed by firearms. And then the building was burnt to cover up the traces of the crime. There are witnesses who survived the massacre and can provide testimony as to exactly what did take place there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you've got two more questions of this witness. You've had the best part of an hour with him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have quite a few questions left, Mr. May, because he has been claiming things that are quite contradictory. Casings are to be found at a place from where one shoots.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Or where one shoots. Where the bullets went, of course, is a different matter. Now, let's move on. You've got two more questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is quite insufficient for me, two questions only.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please. In front of the door, you saw a hole full of casings, 80 by 80. Was that actually a small trench from which there was shooting?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: What door are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I said that you said that in front of the door of the cafe, you saw a hole, 80 by 80, full of casings. Was this a small trench from which there was shooting?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: No, no. You're wrong here. You've been misinformed. There wasn't a trench there. In front of the door, there's a little place where people brush off their shoes before they go in, and that's where the casings were. It wasn't a trench at all. There was no trench or ditch at all there. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please. You actually say that 40 metres away you saw a dried up pool of blood, and you saw that on the 13th of June, that is to say, two months after all the rain and winds and spring and summer and the dogs and the other animals that were there. You saw that two months later. Is that what you saw?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: That's what I said, but you're interpreting it differently. First of all, the massacre of the Berisha family on the 26th was behind the building where the OSCE was. There is where the bloodstains were found. There was also blood where Nexhmedin was injured when he tried to get to the coffee shop from there. You could -- also his clothing was found with blood. It wasn't as you claim it was, as you're interpreting it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the time difference between this event and that 13th of June when you came, how much time had elapsed; two months, two and a half months?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I think the people involved in the autopsies could tell you better how old the bloodstains were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, since you're talking about destroyed houses in Suva Reka, you say, first of all, that - this is point 3 - when you looked at all the events that you processed, out of over 11.000 houses in Suva Reka, over 9.000 were destroyed, and that is over 80 per cent. And then in the next sentence, you say that 1.960 houses were destroyed. So which figure is accurate out of the two?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you, Your Honours, that over a short period, from the 25th of March to the 6th of June, the police and military in the municipality of Suhareke took all sorts of actions, massacring the civilian population on the 25th and the 26th of March at the same time. There was a massacre in the village of Trnje where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, time is short. We really must try and bring this to a close. If you could just concentrate on the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to remind you about the massacres that I had experienced in Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course. We have that in mind. We know your evidence. But the question you were asked was about the houses which were destroyed. Now, how many houses were destroyed? Can you remember or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember, but the most important thing are lives, the human lives, not houses. I'm talking about how many victims died.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, of course we understand that and of course we understand that you have experienced terrible things and your family has and there's a real loss, but you must appreciate this is a criminal trial in which this accused is tried for very serious offences, and time is, for that reason, short. So you must let us be the judges of what is relevant as far as this part of your evidence is concerned. Now, you are being referred to something in your statement, and it says in your statement, dealing with houses, the number is 9.895 out of 11.955 homes destroyed. This makes the percentage of homes destroyed as 83.47 per cent. Then it goes on: "There was a total of 1.960 homes only destroyed." Now, can you clarify what appears to be a discrepancy in the figures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the municipality of Suhareke contains 42 villages, and only one of these villages was not burnt. All the rest were burnt, some of which a hundred per cent. So the first number you mention of 11.000, that's -- 33 per cent of the houses were burnt in the municipality as a total. 1.200 houses, those were the houses in Suhareke, in the city of Suhareke, 1.200.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. We can see what's in the statement. There appears to be a discrepancy of some sort. Now, one final question, because you really have had a good deal of time with this witness. This will be your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say on page 8, item 4, that 21 educational institutions were destroyed and shelled, and in the next sentence, you say that 15 educational institutions were destroyed. So again, this is a considerable discrepancy. Now, all of it put together, how were all these houses, institutions, everything, how was that destroyed? Was it destroyed during war operations or in some other way?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: All that destruction of houses and schools and religious buildings were carried out by the police in their various operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Wladimiroff, have you any questions? No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Mr. May, a question. I'm not going to put a question. I just want to say again that there is a special situation. We have a witness here who is at the same time an amateur investigator, and then in his capacity a witness, he explains what he found out as an investigator dilettante. I think that the other side is really being very imaginative when they bring in such witnesses. I don't know how many roles he is performing right now during this examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is a matter for the Trial Chamber to determine the relevance of his evidence and the weight to be given to it. Now, Mr. Wladimiroff, do you have any questions, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have. Questioned by Mr. Wladimiroff:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I have a few questions that may assist the Court. On page 2 of your statement, you tell about what happened to 10 Albanian civilians from several families after the Serb forces told, on the 22nd of March, that the Serbs had been killing. You say that these 10 Albanians were killed. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, this happened on the 22nd of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you witness that yourself or was that told to you?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: This happened a long way from my house, and during the investigations regarding the bodies, I found out about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find out who killed them and how the killing came about, where exactly they were killed?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. We realised immediately on the 22nd of March in the afternoon that in the old part of Suhareke, in the centre, the Serbian police had entered certain houses and killed civilians. Among them there was a woman of 70.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in thinking that you did not witness what happened there, but you were told by others and you investigated to reconstruct what happened?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: There were witnesses who had survived this incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: If there is need, Your Honour, I can give the names of the witnesses who can testify to this to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a few other questions related to the list you drew up that may assist the Court as well. I'm a little bit confused, because today a list was tendered to the Court called Annex B, Annexure B, but previously there has been a list disclosed to the amici which looks like the same list but, actually, I think it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: May I show the witness that list, Your Honour? I will first show the witness the list that has been tendered today, and then I'll show the witness the list I had in my possession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That, Mr. Berisha, is a list that has been tendered today. I suppose you -- these are the letters by which they were given to me. Then the next list, would you recognise that list? Is that the same list or a different list?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: They are approximately the same. It is merely a matter of the order of the names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, to be precise, Mr. Berisha, on the list that has been tendered today, there are 528 names, and on the other list there are 343 list -- names. So there is some difference, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: There are differences because it was not possible to include all the names of the killed and -- those killed and those who were missing. And meanwhile, we've been able to add some more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I will show you that second list again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to give it again to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you will see that on some pages there is handwriting. Is that your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I will give you the original list again, and please go to the page where you see number 121, 122, 123, on the original list, the list I think that has been tendered today, and compare that to the other list, the same numbers. Do you see any differences?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what these differences are?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: The differences lie in the lists of the massacres in the villages. And meanwhile, a massacre in the village of Savrove has been added, as well as the massacre in Trnje. This has been added.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. If you look to the last column, which are your comments. Is that right? On the right hand of that landscaped list, that column, the last column, these are your comments; is that right? All right. I'll repeat it.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I don't have any translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I will repeat my question. The last column of that landscaped list, there are notes or things have been typed there, handwritten notes and things, words typed there. These are your comments; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. For instance, sometimes the age is not known, and sometimes I put in that -- I put in the age 65 when this has been discovered. And this column states whether someone has been killed or is missing. For instance, you get the date, 21st of March, 1999, and this is information from the family on which date this person was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That brings us to column number 8. There is no 8 on the page in front of you, but if you count each column, you look at column 8 and 9, there you will see the place of killing and the date of killing.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you establish the date of killing? Did you witness the killing or was that told to you? Did you research it on the basis of what people told you, or perhaps you saw documents?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: In some cases I was a witness, and in some cases this was on the basis of the investigations that I conducted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Meaning that people told you and you saw documents or only people told you about the killings?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: These were descriptions by immediate eyewitnesses and members of their families.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, if we go to column 3 and 4, that deals with father's name and surname. Do you see these columns?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you establish that kind of data?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: First, as for the Berishas, they are members of my own family and so I knew who their fathers were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But how did you come about that someone was either missing or killed and, therefore, you came about a name?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: The massacre of the Berishas on the 26th of March took place in four houses. It took place in the family of Musli Berisha --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know. But we've got here a list of more than 500 names, so I'm interested to learn how you established all these names; who was killed where, which date, and who he was.

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: During the inspection of the bodies in 1999 when the international forensic teams were working, at the same time, the bodies were identified. I was a kind of connecting link between the families and the forensic teams of The Hague Tribunal, and all the people who were looking for their loved ones filled in a form, an antemortem form, in which they described the missing person on the last day on which this person was seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's very helpful. Now, I put to you that I have seen reports of the German forensic team, and I came across a number of formula where it was stated, "Name unknown." How would you establish the name of that person if he is on your list?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: The people were identified by the members of their families. The relatives were involved in identifying the bodies. And they had information on how the person appeared on the day of his disappearance, how he was dressed, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present during all those identifications or was this told to you by the family?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: I was always present at the identifications.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That's all I ask, Your Honours. I wonder whether the Court would want me to tender the other list, otherwise perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That could be tendered. 240A, would that be a suitable number?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I make a note that there are yellow stripes on it from my hand, and on the right top you'll find a page numbering that is of my hand as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be 241B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 241B. Thank you. Re-examined by Ms. Romano:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, through your role in the commission, as a chairman for the commission for missing persons in Suva Reka, you conducted virtually a one-man inquiry on the events that happened in your town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: Not only in the town but in the entire municipality of Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as part of your work, you compiled the list that is attached to your statement that contains approximately 5 -- 528 names; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: That was the state of things at the time. Perhaps there are changes now and new facts have emerged and additions have been made, but I don't have another list with me yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the point I want to make, Mr. Berisha. So this was an ongoing project that you're working on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: It is still continuing, and it will continue in the future.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you printed several -- sometimes you printed copies that had the state of your investigation at that particular moment?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Just to clarify with the Chamber, I have both lists here, and the first list, that was one of the drafts that Mr. Berisha provided. And the last draft that he provided and the one that was part of his statement is the one that is attached there with 500 names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Last -- last issue, Mr. Berisha. I think there was confusion about the number of homes destroyed. You made an investigation, and you came up with a number of homes that were destroyed in the municipality of Suva Reka, and also a percentage. I will read it to you again what is in the statement, and I will ask you to clarify perhaps a mistake that there is there. You say that: "The figures for this part of my investigation came from the Directorate for Development and Reconstruction of the Suva Reka Municipality, Suva Reka municipality administration. The number is 9.895 out of 11.955 homes destroyed. This makes the percentage of homes destroyed as 83 per cent." You continue and you say that there is a total of 1.960 homes only destroyed. What you wanted to say what you referred to 1.960 homes?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: This relates only to the town of Suhareke. The second part concerns only the town itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So among the 9.000 homes, 1.900 were exactly from the town of Suva Reka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the rest homes were from all over the municipality?

utterances.speaker: HYSNI BERISHA
utterances.text: The remainder were scattered among the 41 villages of Suhareke municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berisha.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for making it possible for me to describe a part of what has happened to me and the crimes that happened in 1999 in Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honours, we still have time. I have the other witness available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We might as well make a start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Romano:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Mitchell, can you please state to the Court your full name. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sandra Lynne Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your nationality?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: American.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when were you born?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll ask the witness to give a very short description of her background but I would also like to tender her curriculum vitae into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Mitchell, can you please just very briefly give your background to the Court.

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'm a trained attorney and practiced law in the United States for about seven years and then began working in the Balkans, first in Bulgaria, then in Bosnia, Kosovo, Albania, Macedonia, as well as with some of the OSCE institutions in Warsaw and in Vienna. I worked for both non-governmental organisations in the area of human rights as well as for the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe in different missions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Mitchell, you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor a statement dated of 12 May, 2002. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the 2nd of July, 2002, you also attended a meeting here in The Hague with a presiding officer of the Registrar where you confirmed that the contents of your statement are true?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I would like --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One more thing. At that time also you made an addendum where you presented several documents that you brought with you to The Hague; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SANDRA MITCHELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The Prosecution submits the statements and the addendum into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters have one request while there is still time, to mind your speed, especially when reading.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 242, and the statement will be numbered Prosecution Exhibit 243 for the original and 243A for the redacted version. The curriculum vitae is numbered Prosecution Exhibit 242, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I apologise to the translators, interpreters. I'll really try to slow down. Between November 1998 and April 2000, Ms. Mitchell was director of Human Rights Division in the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, OSCE, Kosovo. Prior to this, May-October 1998, she was legal advisor in the OSCE for democratic institutions and human rights. In this capacity, she was assigned to mission planning and deployment team for the Kosovo Verification Mission, KVM.
